question:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine, will the 1-incidence rate ratio overestimate / underestimate / correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy?

Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. underestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the observed incidence rate ratio reflects a mixture of fully protected individuals (who contribute zero events) and completely unprotected ones. Because the protected fraction experiences no exposures at all in the data, the overall rate in the vaccinated arm is pulled downward more than would be expected from a uniform per-exposure reduction. Consequently the 1-IRR ends up smaller than the true per-exposure efficacy that would apply to a susceptible individual on each exposure; i.e., it underestimates that quantity. This is the opposite pattern from a leaky vaccine, where the two measures coincide.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer here is B. underestimate. For an all-or-nothing vaccine, the incidence rate ratio is computed from aggregate person-time data across the whole population, which mixes the fully protected individuals with the unprotected ones. Because exposures are not observed individually, the ratio ends up averaging the zero-risk periods of the protected subset with the full-risk periods of the unprotected subset; this averaging necessarily pulls the apparent efficacy downward relative to the true per-exposure protection that would be measured if every exposure could be tracked separately. The bias is therefore in the direction of underestimation.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: C. correctly estimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the efficacy is binary at the individual level: a recipient is either fully protected against infection from any exposure or derives no protection at all. The incidence rate in the vaccinated arm is therefore simply the incidence rate in the unprotected fraction of that arm. The 1 – incidence-rate-ratio therefore recovers exactly that fraction. Because each exposure is an independent Bernoulli trial whose success probability is zero for the protected individuals and unchanged for the unprotected, the ratio of cumulative incidences (or of incidence rates under constant hazard) equals the per-exposure efficacy parameter; no systematic inflation or deflation occurs. Hence the 1-IRR correctly estimates per-exposure vaccine efficacy.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fraction \(p\) of individuals are fully protected (infection rate exactly 0) while the remainder \(1-p\) remain fully susceptible (infection rate identical to the unvaccinated). Consequently the observed incidence rate in the vaccinated arm equals exactly \((1-p)\) times the unvaccinated rate at every moment, so the incidence-rate ratio equals \(1-p\) and \(1-\text{IRR}=p\). Because the per-exposure efficacy experienced by each individual is either 1 or 0, the population-average per-exposure efficacy is likewise \(p\). The two quantities therefore coincide and \(1-\text{IRR}\) correctly estimates per-exposure vaccine efficacy (answer C).

(The same algebra does not hold for leaky vaccines or for cumulative-incidence ratios, but those cases are outside the question.)

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. underestimate

The key distinction here is between an all-or-nothing vaccine (which completely protects a fraction \(p\) of recipients and leaves the remainder unprotected) and a “leaky” vaccine (which multiplies every recipient’s per-exposure hazard by a constant factor).  

Under a constant external force of infection \(\lambda\), the population incidence rate at calendar time \(t\) equals  
\[
IR_u(t)=\lambda\exp(-\lambda t)\qquad\text{(unvaccinated)}
\]  
\[
IR_v(t)=(1-p)\lambda\exp(-(1-p)\lambda t)\qquad\text{(vaccinated)}.
\]  
Their ratio therefore evolves as  
\[
IRR(t)=(1-p)\exp(p\lambda t).
\]  
At \(t=0\) the ratio equals \(1-p\), but it rises thereafter. Any time-averaged or cumulative IRR observed in a longitudinal study therefore exceeds \(1-p\). Consequently  
\[
1-IRR<p,
\]  
i.e., the usual incidence-rate-ratio estimator understates the true per-exposure efficacy \(p\).

(The same depletion effect does not occur with a leaky vaccine, whose hazard ratio remains constant; thus the bias is specific to the all-or-nothing mechanism.)

Final answer: B. underestimate

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The question concerns estimation of per-exposure VE (i.e., the fraction of individuals rendered completely immune) by the summary 1-IRR when the vaccine is strictly all-or-nothing.  

Under an all-or-nothing model a vaccinated cohort consists of an immune fraction ε and a fully susceptible fraction 1-ε that experiences the same hazard λ as unvaccinated individuals. Because the immune subjects never leave the risk set, the composition of the observed vaccinated risk set becomes progressively enriched for immune individuals. Consequently the instantaneous incidence rate observed among vaccinated subjects at any time t is  

rate_V(t) = λ · [(1-ε)S(t)] / [ε + (1-ε)S(t)] < λ(1-ε),  

where S(t) is the survival function of the susceptible stratum. The inequality implies that the person-time-weighted IRR is strictly smaller than 1-ε, so the derived quantity 1-IRR exceeds the true per-exposure efficacy ε. Hence the 1-IRR overestimates per-exposure VE.  

(The bias vanishes only in the limit of zero cumulative incidence; otherwise it is positive and grows with follow-up time.)

Under standard assumptions of equal exposure distributions, the incidence rate among vaccinated individuals is therefore exactly (1 − VE) times the incidence rate among unvaccinated individuals at every moment. Consequently the incidence-rate ratio equals 1 − VE exactly, and 1 − IRR recovers the true proportion protected without bias. Because the all-or-nothing model contains no partial per-exposure effect, this quantity is also the correct estimate of per-exposure vaccine efficacy. The answer is therefore C.

(The contrast case—a leaky vaccine that multiplies every individual’s per-exposure risk by the same factor—produces a time-varying hazard ratio whose 1 − IRR value does not recover the per-exposure parameter; that distinction is irrelevant here because the vaccine is stipulated to be all-or-nothing.)
